Hi Sanjay / Emily 1

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side based on the discovery: 

Summary of what we heard
- Primary preference: Private VPC deployment (customer-managed VPC) to satisfy data residency and network controls.
- Unclear on PrivateLink vs VPC peering preference  sounds like you may prefer PrivateLink but want to confirm with NetOps.
- Requirement: IP allowlist and strict egress controls; TLS in transit and KMS-managed keys for at-rest encryption.
- Potential need for dedicated capacity (reserved Redwood Dedicated) for predictable throughput  you mentioned spikes from batch jobs.

Questions / Info we need from your NetOps team
1) Do you allow AWS PrivateLink endpoints, or do you prefer VPC peering?
2) Please share VPC IDs, account IDs, and CIDR ranges you plan to use (we typically request a /16 or /20 range for our endpoint subnets).
3) Any corporate proxies or NAT gateways that would affect outbound connectivity?
4) Do you require mutual TLS or will standard TLS server auth suffice?

Attachments: I attached a short design doc (redwood-private-vpc-design.pdf) that outlines both PrivateLink and VPC peering options and the networking primitives we need.

Proposed next steps
- Technical deep-dive with Vivek (cc'd) and your NetOps to lock the connectivity pattern  can we target Tue, Mar 31 for a 45-min call?
- You share the CIDR/VPC/account details ahead of the call (attachment or reply).
- We prepare a scoped deployment plan and procurement checklist (SOW/quote if you want dedicated capacity).

Thanks 1 looking forward to progressing.

Best,

Hi Rajiv / NetOps 1

Thanks for jumping in. I've attached the short design doc again (redwood-private-vpc-design.pdf) that explains both connectivity patterns and what we need for each. To help netops triage, a few notes specific to PrivateLink vs Peering: 

PrivateLink (recommended when allowed)
- We create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in our account and you create an AWS VPC Endpoint Service or we publish a service  common pattern is Redwood publishes an endpoint service and you create an interface endpoint in your VPC.
- Benefits: no route table changes, endpoint traffic stays in AWS backbone, easier security posture for many enterprises.
- Information we need from you: allowed security groups for the ENI, list of allowed VPC endpoint subnets (one per AZ recommended), account ID(s) and region.

VPC Peering (alternate)
- Requires route table updates and mutual route acceptance; good when PrivateLink is disallowed.
- We need peering connections, propagation guidance for transit gateways if you use them, and NAT/egress considerations.

Specific asks for the upcoming technical call
- AWS Account ID(s) and VPC ID(s) + CIDR blocks
- Are there transit/VPN appliances that will inspect or proxy traffic?
- Do you have static egress IPs behind a NAT gateway we should allow in an IP allowlist?
- Confirm whether you can create interface endpoints in your VPC (PrivateLink).

Can we confirm Tue, Mar 31 at 11:00 PT for the technical deep-dive with Vivek? If that works, I'll send a calendar invite and include a short agenda.

Thanks,

Hi Rajiv / team 1

Quick technical notes ahead of tomorrow's call. I want to surface practical constraints and the exact items we'll need from NetOps so the meeting is productive.

If you choose PrivateLink (preferred path):
- We will provide an AWS Account ID and create an NLB that front-ends the Redwood inference runtime. You will create interface endpoints in your VPC pointing at our service.
- Security groups on the interface endpoint must allow outbound TCP 443 to the NLB. For IP allowlisting we recommend securing at the SG level; there is no stable source IP for PrivateLink ENIs (they are in your VPC), so SG-based controls + endpoint policies are best.
- We will need the endpoint subnet IDs (one per AZ) where you will create the interface endpoints.

If you choose VPC peering (alternate):
- We'll need peering connection setup and route table entries. Peering exposes a set of IPs for our service; we can provide a documented list of service IPs per region (note: ranges can change during maintenance windows  we'll communicate changes).
- NAT/egress: if your VPC uses a centralized NAT, ensure the route to Redwood endpoints isn't routed through a proxy that will terminate TLS in the middle unless you require that.

Other items we need from you before we start provisioning:
- AWS Account ID(s) and VPC ID(s) (for all regions you plan to use).
- VPC CIDR(s) and preferred endpoint subnet(s)  suggested: /24 per endpoint subnet per AZ.
- Names of any transit gateways or firewalls that traffic will traverse.
- Desired TLS model: TLS server cert only, or mTLS? If mTLS, we'll coordinate cert exchange (we support client certs via our gateway).

For Dedicated capacity consideration:
- If you expect sustained RPS above ~200/s or heavy KV cache usage, dedicated pools make the most sense. We can include a capacity sizing template in the follow-up SOW.

Happy to go through packet flow diagrams on the call. If you can paste Account ID(s) and a short list of endpoint subnets ahead of the call that will save time.

Thanks,
Vivek Kulkarni
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
